claims.text: Enhancing formation of a thin, thermally reinforced iron oxide surface layer can suppress corrosion degradation of Q235 steel.
The proposed thermal treatment accelerates formation of a protective iron oxide film before environmental exposure.
The thermally formed protective film is primarily Fe2O3.
Thermal treatment stabilizes the protective iron oxide film.
The treatment produces a continuous and adherent passive oxide layer.
A continuous oxide layer reduces the area of active metal exposed to the corrosive medium.
Enhanced oxidation kinetics create a uniform, slightly thickened iron oxide layer.
The thermally formed oxide layer is mechanically robust and chemically inert.
Elevated temperatures favor stabilization of the oxide film.
Reducing exposed active-metal area slows anodic dissolution and the overall corrosion reaction rate.
Thermally pretreated Q235 steel will have lower mass loss than untreated Q235 steel under otherwise identical exposure conditions.
Thermally pretreated Q235 steel will develop fewer localized corrosion sites than untreated steel.
Thermally pretreated Q235 steel will exhibit a more uniform oxide morphology than untreated steel.
Corrosion suppression by the treatment will be more pronounced at elevated temperature than at room temperature.
The proposed effect applies where the environment initiates corrosion but still permits passivation, including moderate-chloride conditions up to about 200 °C.
Environments that completely destroy the oxide layer and extremely high temperatures fall outside the proposed mechanism's domain.
A controlled comparison will expose thermally treated and untreated Q235 samples to identical saline environments at room and elevated temperatures.
Failure to obtain statistically lower mass loss and pitting, together with improved impedance, under both temperature regimes would falsify the hypothesis.
